analysis.one_liner: Raises the investment-income tax on the wealthiest private colleges' endowments from 1.4% to 35%.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would multiply by 25 the existing tax on investment earnings of the very largest private university endowments. Today, private colleges pay a 1.4% tax on their endowment investment income; under this bill, any private, non-religious institution with more than $10 billion in assets would pay 35% instead. Only a handful of the nation's wealthiest universities would qualify. The money would go to the general Treasury; the bill does not earmark it for any specific use.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers as a whole, indirectly, through new revenue collected from a handful of elite university endowments and deposited in the general Treasury. No individual or group gets a direct benefit; the gain is reduced deficits or whatever Congress later chooses to fund with the money.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the excise tax on net investment income from 1.4% to 35% for private educational institutions that are not religious in nature and whose assets were worth at least $10 billion in the prior year.
The higher rate would apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2023, if enacted.
Because only institutions above the $10 billion asset threshold qualify, the tax falls on a small number of the nation's richest endowments rather than on colleges broadly.

analysis.who_pays: The few private universities with endowments and other assets exceeding $10 billion, which would owe 35% on their net investment income instead of 1.4% — potentially hundreds of millions to more than a billion dollars a year each at the largest schools. Endowment returns at these schools fund scholarships, research, and operations, so a smaller after-tax return could squeeze those budgets.

drawbacks.text: The $10 billion asset threshold means only a small handful of universities would ever owe the tax, so the bill raises relatively modest revenue and functions as a targeted levy on a few well-known institutions rather than a broad tax principle.

The bill exempts religious institutions, so a religious college with an equally large endowment would keep the 1.4% rate — a line that critics could call arbitrary and that raises constitutional questions about differential treatment.

Endowment investment income is what funds much of the need-based financial aid, research, and operating budgets at wealthy private universities; a 35% tax on those returns would leave less for those purposes, and schools might respond by cutting aid, raising tuition, or shifting investments. The bill includes no requirement that affected schools absorb the cost rather than pass it on to students.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary people is real but diffuse: new revenue to the Treasury with no dedicated use, and only from a handful of institutions. The cost is concentrated on the affected universities and potentially their students, since a large tax on endowment returns could squeeze scholarship and research budgets at exactly the schools with the most generous aid. Weighing honestly, this is a populist-framed tax increase whose public payoff depends entirely on what Congress later does with the money — and it was never seriously advanced, so its design was never tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2023, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator J.D. Vance introduced the bill in the Senate on December 14, 2023.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the standard first step for a tax bill.
The action history shows no further action — no committee hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, at which point the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The handful of universities with $10 billion-plus endowments are better off: they keep paying the 1.4% rate on their investment income instead of the proposed 35%. No one else gained — the bill raised no revenue because it never became law.

for.name: Sen. J.D. Vance
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it to the Senate Finance Committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the thirteen months remaining in the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration; the bill's only actions were introduction and referral.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill, so no party split is recorded; it was introduced by a single Republican senator and drew zero cosponsors from either party, suggesting it never had broad support in either caucus.

industries.industry: Elite private universities (those with $10 billion+ endowments)
industries.note: These institutions would have owed a 35% tax on endowment investment income instead of the current 1.4%, reducing after-tax returns that fund scholarships, research, and operations. Their interest in the bill's failure was keeping that money, which is the same revenue the bill would have directed to the Treasury.
